opus-5.5.text:
I think it depends on what you mean by "bubble." If a bubble means valuations and expectations are running ahead of what the technology can deliver right now, then yes, I think there's definitely some of that. A lot of money is flowing in, and many companies are raising at valuations that assume general-purpose robots will be in homes and factories within a few years. Honestly, I don't think the technology is there yet.

But I'd distinguish this from a bubble where there's nothing underneath. What's different this time is that there's real technical progress. Before large models, every robot task was its own engineering project. You'd spend months on one skill, and it wouldn't transfer to anything else. Now, with vision-language-action models and foundation models for robotics, we're seeing generalization for the first time: a robot following instructions it never saw in training, handling objects it never touched. That's a qualitative change, and I've worked in this field long enough to feel how different it is.

So the way I judge it is to look at the gap between the demos and the deployments. Demos are getting very impressive, but most are carefully set up, in controlled environments, and often teleoperated or cherry-picked. The real test is reliability. A robot that succeeds 90% of the time makes a great video, but in a real home or factory you need 99.9%, and that last stretch is incredibly hard. When companies start showing robots working for long hours in unstructured environments, at a cost that makes economic sense, the valuations will start to be justified.

The other thing I watch is data. Language models had the whole internet. Robotics doesn't have an equivalent, and nobody has fully solved how to get robot data at that scale, whether through teleoperation, simulation, human videos, or some combination. Until that's solved, I think progress will be real but slower than the hype suggests.

So my view is that there's froth, and some companies won't survive. But much like the internet bubble, the underlying trend is real. Even if there's a correction, I think embodied intelligence will be one of the most important things we build in the next decade or two. The question isn't whether it'll happen, but whether the timelines people are pricing in are realistic, and I think many of them are too optimistic.

r001.rationale: The response says progress is real but slower than the hype and that current technology cannot yet meet priced-in timelines, making development pace a determinant.

r002.rationale: It says valuations depend on robots working reliably for long hours in unstructured homes or factories at an economically viable cost.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I get asked a lot, and honestly, I don't think there's a clean yes or no answer. Let me try to separate a few things.

First, is there a bubble in valuations? Probably, in parts of it. When you see companies with a demo video and no revenue raising at multi-billion valuations, that's a signal that capital is moving faster than the technology. I've been in this field long enough to remember when robotics couldn't raise money at all, so I'm aware of how much the mood has swung.

But a bubble in money is different from a bubble in the underlying technology. And on the technology side, I actually think the progress is real. Something fundamentally changed in the last few years. For most of robotics history, we were writing controllers by hand, task by task. If you wanted a robot to do a new thing, you basically started over. What's different now is that we can train policies from data, and more importantly, we've seen that these policies can start to generalize. A robot trained on one set of tasks can show some competence on tasks it hasn't seen. That was almost unthinkable ten years ago. So the excitement isn't coming from nowhere.

The way I personally judge it is to look at a few indicators. One is: are the demos getting more honest? In a bubble, demos get more cherry-picked and teleoperated and the gap between the video and reality widens. When I see teams publishing success rates, failure cases, and letting people test robots live, that tells me the field is maturing rather than inflating. Second, I look at whether the cost curves are moving. Hardware getting cheaper, data collection getting cheaper, inference getting cheaper. Those are the things that eventually let a technology become a business, not just a research project. And third, I ask whether anyone is actually paying for it. Not pilots, not partnerships, but repeated deployments where a customer renews because the robot does useful work.

Right now, if I'm honest, the third one is still weak. Most of the value is still in the future. That means a lot of today's companies will not survive, and a lot of investors will lose money. So in that narrow sense, yes, there's a bubble.

But I'd also say that almost every transformative technology went through a phase like this. The internet in 1999 was a bubble and also real. I think robotics is in a similar place. The question that matters to me is not whether the bubble pops, but whether the technology keeps improving through the correction. And from what I see in the research, I think it will. The learning-based approach has a lot of room left. We're nowhere near the ceiling on data, on model scale, or on how we combine simulation with real-world experience.

So my honest answer is: overheated in capital, under-delivered in deployment, but real in the fundamentals. If you're building, the right strategy is to assume the money will get harder and make sure the robot actually works.

r001.rationale: The response uses the pace of technological progress to judge the bubble, contrasting capital moving faster than the technology with real progress and asking whether robotics will keep improving.

r002.rationale: It treats repeated customer deployments and renewals for useful work as a key indicator of whether robotics has viable real-world uses.

astra-6.text:
I’d separate two questions: is the technology making real progress, and are expectations getting ahead of what it can deliver commercially? Both can be true at the same time.

For me, the strongest signal is whether customers keep paying after the pilot. A demo can show that a robot performs a task once. A business needs it to perform reliably, day after day, at a cost that makes sense. That cost includes maintenance, human intervention, integration, and downtime—not just the price of the robot.

So I would look at repeat orders, actual utilization, and how much support each deployment needs. If those are improving, there is substance behind the excitement. If investment and valuations rise while deployments remain mostly demonstrations, I’d be more concerned about a bubble.

I also wouldn’t judge all of robotics together. Different applications have very different economics. There could be excessive speculation in one area and a healthy business in another. The key question is: how much useful work is being done, and does someone find it valuable enough to pay for it?

r001.rationale: It asks whether the technology is making real progress, but does not identify the pace or speed of robot development as a determinant.

r002.rationale: It ties bubble risk to whether robots have economically viable applications, citing repeat orders, utilization, support needs, and customers paying for useful work.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d separate two questions: Is robotics going to create a lot of value, and are today’s expectations getting ahead of what the technology can deliver? Those can both be true.

For me, the most useful signal is whether customers keep paying after the pilot. A demo shows that a robot can do something once. A deployment has to show that it can do it reliably, day after day, at a cost that makes sense. You have to include maintenance, human intervention, integration—all of that.

So I’d look at repeat orders, how much useful work the robots actually perform, and whether the economics improve as deployments grow. If investment and valuations rise much faster than those indicators, that’s a sign of a bubble.

But I wouldn’t judge the entire industry as one thing. Some applications may already have a solid business case, while others depend on breakthroughs that are still uncertain. The key question is: are we pricing in demonstrated progress, or assuming that every remaining problem will be solved very soon?

r001.rationale: The response discusses demonstrated progress and uncertain breakthroughs, but does not identify the pace of robot development as a determinant.

r002.rationale: It says some applications may have a solid business case while others remain uncertain, and ties bubble concerns to deployment economics and customer demand.
